figure: Figure 26.1 (Workload fingerprints on the six axes; in-figure title 'Each family peaks on a different axis')
issue: The in-figure title and the caption both assert 'each family peaks on a different axis', but the drawn bars contradict this: each of the three families is the maximum on TWO axes, not one, so the six axes partition 2-2-2 across the families rather than mapping 1:1 as the headline implies. A careful reader checking each group will find the title literally false.
evidence: Reading the bar heights per group: Context length max = Long-context RAG Q&A (~0.95) and Quality required max = Long-context RAG Q&A (~0.70) -> RAG peaks on 2 axes. Traffic volume max = High-throughput chat (~0.95) and Latency sensitive max = High-throughput chat (~0.90) -> chat peaks on 2 axes. Cost sensitive max = Batch inference (~0.85) and Output tokens max = Batch inference (~0.90) -> batch peaks on 2 axes. No family is the unique peak on a single exclusive axis in the 1:1 sense the title states; each wins a pair, and the pairs are disjoint.
acceptance_test: Make the headline consistent with the bars by either (a) rewording the in-figure title AND the caption to the actual structure, e.g. 'each family peaks on a distinct pair of axes' / 'the six axes split into three family-specific pairs', or (b) adjusting the authored intensities so that exactly three axes have a unique single-family maximum and the remaining three do not, making the original wording literally true. After the edit, a reader who inspects all six groups must find the title's claim consistent with the drawn maxima.
